messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum Reeves is a 32-year-old married man of British descent who works as a private tutor in the suburbs of Portland, Oregon. He presented for assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 59, describing a constellation of symptoms that had been building steadily over the eighteen months since he was stalked by a former tutoring client — a situation that began as unsettling and escalated, over several months, into something that left him fundamentally altered in how he understood the world and his place within it.

The stalking began gradually. A parent of one of Callum's students started appearing at locations he hadn't mentioned — outside the coffee shop where he prepared lesson plans, in the parking lot of his gym, eventually idling on his residential street on a motorcycle, the engine cutting out just as Callum reached his front door. The man never made overt threats; he simply watched. When Callum reported the behaviour, the response from authorities was slow and the legal process inconclusive. The stalker's demeanour throughout — eerily calm, almost pleasant — meant that Callum began to doubt his own perception of danger. By the time a restraining order was finally issued, the damage was done. What frightened Callum most, in retrospect, was not any single incident but the realisation that someone could study him, know his patterns, and present an ordinary face to the world while doing so.

That realisation reshaped how Callum read other people entirely. He had come to believe that people are not what they seem — that the surface presentation of a person reveals nothing reliable about their intentions. When, in his tutoring sessions, a parent raises their voice even slightly, or expresses frustration in what anyone else might consider a measured tone, Callum finds himself scanning for threat: the tightened jaw, the shift in posture, the controlled anger that he now reads as a precursor to something worse. These moments of perceived anger, however ordinary, pull him back into the logic of the stalking — reinforcing his conviction that people cannot be trusted and that he himself cannot reliably judge who is safe. The cycle feeds itself: the more his appraisals of others darken, the more triggers he finds in ordinary social exchanges, and the more ordinary social exchanges become potential triggers.

Callum works from home most days, and the suburban streets outside his window have become a landscape of threat. The sound of a motorcycle engine — common enough in his neighbourhood — reliably produces a jolt of alarm that he describes as indistinguishable from the feeling of being watched. He avoids unfamiliar locations because, as he puts it, he cannot assess the danger when he doesn't know the exits, the sightlines, the patterns of movement. This hypervigilance keeps him in a state of chronic readiness that makes sleep nearly impossible; he lies awake cataloguing sounds, and the exhaustion that follows further erodes his capacity to distinguish genuine threat from false alarm. He frequently reacts as though he is in danger when nothing is actually wrong — a response he recognises intellectually but cannot override.

The strategies Callum has adopted to manage this state have, over time, made it worse. He avoids relaxing deliberately, having concluded that lowering his guard is what allowed the stalking to take hold in the first place. This refusal to rest sustains a baseline of physiological arousal that keeps him primed to detect threat in stimuli that would otherwise pass unnoticed. He has also pulled back emotionally from his wife, Nadia, telling himself that closeness is a vulnerability he can no longer afford — that people cannot be trusted, and this extends, in his darker moments, even to her. Most troublingly, he has developed a pattern of punitive self-talk, telling himself that he deserves to suffer for having failed to recognise the danger sooner. This belief — that his own judgment is fundamentally untrustworthy — compounds his distrust of others and leaves him caught between suspicion of the world and contempt for himself.

What finally brought Callum to seek help was a session with a fifteen-year-old student whose father arrived early and waited in the hallway. Callum heard footsteps pacing and spent the remainder of the hour unable to teach. He cancelled the following week's sessions and told Nadia he thought he was losing his mind. He came to the intake appointment hoping, cautiously, that something could be recovered — though he was not certain he deserved it.
